newsitem.title: USA: Stocks set another record as bond rates tumble.
newsitem.headline: Stocks set another record as bond rates tumble.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks jumped to their fifth straight record Thursday, as bond interest rates tumbled on surprisingly weak economic data that eased concerns about rising interest rates.
The dollar leaped nearly three yen after Japanese officials played down signs of U.S.-Japanese trade frictions and chances for an imminent rise in Japan's interest rates.
The Dow Jones industrial average surged 135.64 points to a record 7,711.47. The index closed above 7,500 for the first time only on Tuesday, and ended at 7,575.83 on Wednesday.
In the broader market, advances outpaced declines 1,868 to 729 on volume of 592.7 million on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index rose 3.47 points to 1,411.32.
The catalyst for the rally came from the bond market, where interest rates tumbled after fresh data suggested the economy has slowed from its torrid first-quarter pace.

The benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury rose 26/32, or $8.125 on a $1,000 bond, reducing its yield to 6.78 percent from 6.84 percent at Wednesday's close. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.

Analysts said the data, which included a surprising decline in U.S. retail sales over the last three months and a higher-than-expected level of weekly jobless claims, proved U.S. economic growth remains within the Federal Reserve's -- and therefore the market's -- comfort zone.

"The combination of those two numbers led people to believe the economy is decelerating and the Fed is on hold at its upcoming meeting," said Phil Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management. "This is Nirvana."

The Fed raised short-term rates in March, the first increase in more than two years, in a bid to slow the economy and ward off inflation. The central bank's policy-makers held rates steady after meeting late last month.

The stock market's rally, coupled with very heavy volume that approached 600 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange, left the impression that investors were almost tripping over themselves to join the advance.

"We now have all the fence-sitters jumping in," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "I had figured we'd pause at 7,500, but here we are two days later and 200 points higher."
The dollar had jumped a staggering 4-1/2 yen in Asia -- from a low of 111.20 yen to 115.70, and staged an impressive recovery in New York after hitting a seven-month low of 110.52 yen on Wednesday.
The dollar backed off a bit but fetched 114.27 yen in late trading, vs. 111.15 late Wednesday. It rose to 1.7290 German marks from 1.7164.

Wheat prices fell after the Agriculture Department said the United States would harvest its biggest crop in three years. At the Chicago Board of Trade, wheat for July delivery closed 11-1/2 cents a bushel lower at $3.53, just above the 4-month low of $3.51 reached on June 5.
Corn and soybean prices also closed mostly lower as the outlook for bumper crops this fall improved. December corn fell 1-1/4 cents to $2.54-1/4 a bushel and November soybeans fell 2 cents to $6.71.
Overseas, London's FTSE 100 closed at 4,757.4, up 32.6 points, or 0.69 percent. In Tokyo, the 225-share Nikkei average closed at 20,564.46, up 274.53 points, or 1.35 percent.
